questions.q: What three labels does McGee use to sort the worries people have?
a: Historical, hysterical and helpful
Real, imagined and inherited
Past, present and future
Useful, useless and urgent
questions.why: The summary sorts every worry into one of three buckets, historical, hysterical or helpful, depending on its root cause.

questions.q: How does the summary describe the relationship between worry and anxiety?
a: Each one feeds the other in a repeating loop
Anxiety always comes first and worry follows
Worry stops anxiety once you name it
The two are unrelated but both harmful
questions.why: Worry triggers the body's survival response, and the resulting anxiety creates more worry, forming a feedback loop.

questions.q: What is the root of a historical worry, according to McGee?
a: A bad memory or experience from your past
A rare disaster you read about online
A real deadline coming up at work
A fear passed down from your parents
questions.why: Historical worries trace back to something that actually happened to you, such as being mugged on a dark street.

questions.q: What does McGee suggest doing with a hysterical worry?
a: Check the evidence and see how unlikely it is
Plan every detail of the worst case
Revisit the memory until it fades
Distract yourself whenever it appears
questions.why: Hysterical worries are irrational, so the summary says to examine the evidence and then let them go.

questions.q: On the author's zero-to-ten scale, what does a zero mean?
a: You have no control over the outcome
You are certain the outcome is bad
You have already solved the problem
You should stop worrying at once
questions.why: The scale measures how much influence you have; zero means none, while ten means you can shape the result.
